ACCPPDE101: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
BENBUSI211: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.
BENENTR211: Marketing & Consumer Engagement examines consumer psychology, marketing strategy, responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students analyse a company strategy, design a brand and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Digital marketing and customer-journey mapping connect analysis with practical recommendations.
BENENTR212: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
BENENTR311: Market Research explores how companies learn about customer preferences. Students plan and carry out research, analyse their findings and present how those findings can inform business decisions.
BENENTR312: Examines how trade, globalisation and political, cultural and technological conditions shape international business decisions. Students analyse governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate a business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices.
BENGATE101: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
BENGATE102: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.
BENLEAD112: Studies leadership communication through theory, persuasion, emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Students analyse literary characters, film and speeches, interview a leader, prepare a communication advisory report, and develop an address explaining their own ethical leadership vision.
BENLEAD211: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.
BENLEAD311: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations. Case discussions and research-based frameworks address motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture, power, conflict and change.
BENLEAD312: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
DISARIN111: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.
DISDATA111: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
DISDATA212: Image Processing & Computer Vision studies how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognise structures and objects. Topics include colour, image statistics, filtering, segmentation, feature detection, tracking and object classification. Practical work uses Python and OpenCV to develop and benchmark an image-recognition pipeline on previously unseen images.
DISDATA311: Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python, Keras and TensorFlow implementations. Students build and train networks, study backpropagation, regularisation and model evaluation, and apply deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects investigate prediction problems and report experimental results.
DISGATE101: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
DISGATE102: Mathematical Methods develops foundational techniques in differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica. A project implements, analyses and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and computational results.
GOSSOCI111: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
GOSSOCI212: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
GOSSOCI214: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
GOSSOCI311: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.
HCBPSYC111: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
HCBPSYC315: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
MCCCOMM111: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.
MCCCOMM211: Style & Meaning studies stylistics: how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts and also in nonfiction. Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.
MCCCOMM212: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
MCCCOMM213: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
MCCCOMM311: Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.
MCCMEDI111: Introduction to Film & Media examines how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema and major movements with feminist and postcolonial interpretation, alongside television, digital platforms and spectatorship. An analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory and scholarly research.
MCCMEDI112: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
MCCMEDI211: From T.V. to TikTok examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Television, film and digital forms connect storytelling and power with identity and imagined futures. Students compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, investigate disability representation, and develop futures-oriented creative projects.
MCCMEDI212: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
MCCMEDI311: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
MCCMEDI312: Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
